title: Despair not
hook: despair not of God's mercy, for God forgives all sins (Quran 39:53)
carry: even if your sins reached the clouds

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Nickel Mines, and neighbors at a grieving door. Your line was the other family.

Two in the morning, and somebody is awake, replaying something they did years ago. A word said in anger. A friend let down. A thing nobody else knows. Others may have forgiven or forgotten it. Not the one lying awake. There's a voice in that kind of night that says: too late, too much, this one stays. The Qur'an has a verse spoken straight into that voice. It doesn't start with a rule. It starts by naming the people it's talking to.
screen: `AWAKE AT TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `TOO LATE, TOO MUCH.` → `A VERSE SPOKEN INTO THAT VOICE.`

segments.voice: First, who it's for. The verse opens with a command to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to speak in God's name. In Pickthall's translation: "Say: O My slaves who have been prodigal to their own hurt!" Prodigal here means people who have gone too far, wasting themselves, hurting their own souls. Notice the word My. Not those people: My slaves, belonging to God. The ones who went too far are still addressed as His. Second, the command. "Despair not of the mercy of Allah." What's forbidden, at least in this line, isn't the wrong. It's despair. The verse treats hopelessness about mercy as its own kind of mistake, as if to say the door is not the problem; believing it's locked is. Third, the reach. "Who forgiveth all sins." All. The next verse calls people to turn to their Lord and surrender to Him before a reckoning comes, and the promise is read together with that turning back. Read that way, mercy isn't a reason to stop caring. It's a reason not to give up. Fourth, the name. The verse ends: "Lo! He is the Forgiving, the Merciful." The Forgiving, in Arabic, is al-Ghafur, one of the names Muslims use for God. A saying of the Prophet, recorded by at-Tirmidhi, puts it vividly: in it God says that even if a person's sins reached the clouds of the sky, and they asked forgiveness, God would forgive them. For Muslims who pray with this verse, it answers the voice that says too late with two words: despair not.
screen: `O MY SLAVES: STILL CALLED MINE.` · `DESPAIR IS WHAT'S FORBIDDEN.` · `ALL SINS, AND A TURNING BACK.` · `THE FORGIVING, THE MERCIFUL.` · then, large: `DESPAIR NOT OF THE MERCY OF ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Let one old guilt come up, something already done that you've said sorry for or can't fix now, and hold it the way the verse holds its listeners: as someone who went too far and is still called by name. When the voice says it's too late, don't argue; just set the verse's two words beside it, despair not, and let the weight loosen a little, even if it doesn't leave. If you pray, you can ask forgiveness in your own tradition's words.
Al-Ghafur. The Forgiving, a name for God in Islam, from the verse that tells those who went too far: despair not. Today's word.
Your line: even if your sins reached the clouds. Still called by name. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims seek God's forgiveness, called istighfar, in prayer and in their own words, and call on God by names such as al-Ghafur, the Forgiving.

chat.says: What does that Qur'an verse about despair actually tell people?
options: Don't despair of God's mercy; the ones who went too far are still called His.
That despair is a sign the person was never sincere in the first place.
That mercy means you don't need to turn back or care anymore.
chat.meaning: Qur'an 39:53 forbids despair of God's mercy and still calls those who went too far My slaves. It's read together with the next verse's turning back.

notes: Muslim voices begin here (days 956 on). The review notes the shift from the Christian voices.

Pickthall 1930 wording of 39:53 should be checked word for word ('Say: O My slaves who have been prodigal to their own hurt! Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins. Lo! He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.').
Hadith qudsi on sins reaching the clouds of the sky (anan as-sama'), paraphrased: confirm the number Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3540 and the wording.
'Prodigal, here, means people who have gone too far, wasting themselves' is a gloss on Pickthall's English, not an Arabic etymology; confirm.
Muslim scholars also teach that wrongs against other people require making amends with them; the voice doesn't raise it, as tomorrow and later Muslim days may. A Keeper may want a line on it.
'Al-Ghafur, one of the names Muslims use for God' makes no count of the names on purpose.
